claim: Acetylcholine (ACh), released in the hippocampus from fibers originating in the medial septum/diagonal band of Broca (MSDB) complex, is crucial for learning and memory.
source: Acetylcholine (ACh), released in the hippocampus from fibers originating in the medial septum/diagonal band of Broca (MSDB) complex, is crucial for learning and memory.
evidence: This is a general statement about ACh's role in learning and memory, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The CA2 region of the hippocampus has received increasing attention in the context of social memory.
source: The CA2 region of the hippocampus has received increasing attention in the context of social memory.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus about the CA2 region's role in social memory.

claim: MSDB cholinergic neurons inhibition impairs social novelty discrimination in mice.
source: Specifically, MSDB cholinergic neurons inhibition impairs social novelty discrimination, meaning the propensity of a mouse to interact with a novel rather than a familiar conspecific.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral effects of MSDB cholinergic neuron inhibition.

claim: A selective antagonist of nicotinic AChRs delivered in CA2 mimics the effect of MSDB cholinergic neurons inhibition on social novelty discrimination.
source: This effect is mimicked by a selective antagonist of nicotinic AChRs delivered in CA2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that pharmacological blockade of nicotinic receptors in CA2 produces similar behavioral effects.

claim: Activation of nAChRs by nicotine increases the excitatory drive to CA2 principal cells via disinhibition.
source: Ex vivo recordings from hippocampal slices provide insight into the underlying mechanism, as activation of nAChRs by nicotine increases the excitatory drive to CA2 principal cells via disinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from hippocampal slices showing the mechanism of nicotine action.

claim: Optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons in MSDB increases the firing of CA2 principal cells in vivo.
source: In line with this observation, optogenetic activation of cholinergic neurons in MSDB increases the firing of CA2 principal cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiological recordings showing increased firing rates upon optogenetic stimulation.

claim: nAChRs are essential players in social novelty discrimination by controlling inhibition in the CA2 region.
source: These results point to nAChRs as essential players in social novelty discrimination by controlling inhibition in the CA2 region.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dysfunction of the cholinergic system contributes to cognitive impairments associated with several neuropsychiatric diseases including neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Dysfunction of the cholinergic system contributes to cognitive impairments associated with several neuropsychiatric diseases including neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders (Deutsch et al., 2016; Hampel et al., 2018; Perez-Lloret and Barrantes, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on cholinergic dysfunction in neuropsychiatric diseases.

claim: The medial septum/diagonal band of Broca complex (MSDB) in the basal forebrain provides the major cholinergic innervation to the hippocampus through the fimbria–fornix pathway.
source: The medial septum/diagonal band of Broca complex (MSDB) in the basal forebrain provides the major cholinergic innervation to the hippocampus through the fimbria–fornix pathway (for review see Dutar et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article on cholinergic innervation of the hippocampus.

claim: ACh is released from cholinergic terminals via both wired and volume transmission.
source: ACh, released from cholinergic terminals via both wired and volume transmission, targets nicotinic and muscarinic receptors (nAChRs and mAChRs) differently distributed in subcellular domains and cell types across the hippocampal layers (Umbriaco et al., 1995; Sarter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ACh release mechanisms.

claim: Nicotinic and muscarinic receptors are differently distributed in subcellular domains and cell types across the hippocampal layers.
source: ACh, released from cholinergic terminals via both wired and volume transmission, targets nicotinic and muscarinic receptors (nAChRs and mAChRs) differently distributed in subcellular domains and cell types across the hippocampal layers (Umbriaco et al., 1995; Sarter et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on receptor distribution.

claim: Local ACh concentration is controlled by the hydrolytic action of acetylcholinesterase.
source: Activation of nAChRs and mAChRs, which relies on local ACh concentration controlled by the hydrolytic action of acetylcholinesterase (Vijayan, 1979), leads to complex effects on neuronal excitability, synaptic plasticity, rhythmic oscillations, brain states, and behavior (for review see Teles-Grilo Ruivo and Mellor, 2013; Dannenberg et al., 2017; Haam and Yakel, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on acetylcholinesterase function.

claim: The dorsal CA2 and the ventral CA1 hippocampal regions have been associated with social memory.
source: Recently, the dorsal CA2 and the ventral CA1 hippocampal regions have been associated with social memory, which in rodents can be assessed as the capacity of the animal to discriminate between novel and familiar individuals (Stevenson and Caldwell, 2014; Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Okuyama et al., 2016; Raam et al., 2017; for review see Dudek et al., 2016; Piskorowski and Chevaleyre, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research on hippocampal regions and social memory.

claim: The CA2 receives substantial cholinergic innervation from the MSDB.
source: Like other hippocampal subfields, the CA2 receives substantial cholinergic innervation from the MSDB (Cui et al., 2013; Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014; Kohara et al., 2014); however, the potential role of ACh in social memory has not been explored yet.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on cholinergic innervation of CA2.

claim: ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB are activated in response to social stimuli.
source: Here, we report that ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB are activated in response to social stimuli, and that selective inhibition of cholinergic neurons in the MSDB or cholinergic fibers in the dorsal CA2 hippocampal region impairs social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing c-Fos expression in ChAT+ neurons following social interaction.

claim: Selective inhibition of cholinergic fibers in the dorsal CA2 hippocampal region impairs social novelty discrimination.
source: Here, we report that ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB are activated in response to social stimuli, and that selective inhibition of cholinergic neurons in the MSDB or cholinergic fibers in the dorsal CA2 hippocampal region impairs social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing behavioral impairments following local inhibition of cholinergic fibers in CA2.

claim: ACh controls social novelty discrimination via nAChRs but not mAChRs.
source: This effect is mimicked by local delivery of nAChRs but not mAChRs blockers, suggesting a key role of ACh in controlling social novelty discrimination, via nAChRs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential effects of nicotinic versus muscarinic receptor antagonists on social behavior.

claim: mCherry was expressed in cells bodies of neurons in the MSDB following AAV-DIO-ChR2-mCherry virus injection.
source: mCherry was expressed in cells bodies of neurons in the MSDB (Figure 1B) and in cholinergic fibers targeting different hippocampal areas (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cholinergic fibers expressing mCherry target different hippocampal areas.
source: mCherry was expressed in cells bodies of neurons in the MSDB (Figure 1B) and in cholinergic fibers targeting different hippocampal areas (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is high cholinergic fiber density in molecular layer (ML), CA2 and CA3 regions as compared to CA1 and DG.
source: Macroscopic inspection and quantitative analysis revealed a high cholinergic fiber density in molecular layer (ML), CA2 and CA3 regions as compared to CA1 and DG (Figure 1D-E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative analysis of cholinergic fiber density shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Septal cholinergic axon density in DG is 8.73 ± 1.1.
source: Quantification of septal cholinergic axon densities in the DG, ML, CA3, CA2, and CA1 regions (n = 4 animals; four hippocampal slices/animal; DG: 8.73 ± 1.1; ML: 42.3 ± 8.8; CA3: 46.3 ± 5.3; CA2: 48.2 ± 8.6; CA1: 14.6 ± 3.5; p = 0.0006; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1E.

claim: Septal cholinergic axon density in ML is 42.3 ± 8.8.
source: Quantification of septal cholinergic axon densities in the DG, ML, CA3, CA2, and CA1 regions (n = 4 animals; four hippocampal slices/animal; DG: 8.73 ± 1.1; ML: 42.3 ± 8.8; CA3: 46.3 ± 5.3; CA2: 48.2 ± 8.6; CA1: 14.6 ± 3.5; p = 0.0006; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1E.

claim: Septal cholinergic axon density in CA3 is 46.3 ± 5.3.
source: Quantification of septal cholinergic axon densities in the DG, ML, CA3, CA2, and CA1 regions (n = 4 animals; four hippocampal slices/animal; DG: 8.73 ± 1.1; ML: 42.3 ± 8.8; CA3: 46.3 ± 5.3; CA2: 48.2 ± 8.6; CA1: 14.6 ± 3.5; p = 0.0006; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1E.

claim: Septal cholinergic axon density in CA2 is 48.2 ± 8.6.
source: Quantification of septal cholinergic axon densities in the DG, ML, CA3, CA2, and CA1 regions (n = 4 animals; four hippocampal slices/animal; DG: 8.73 ± 1.1; ML: 42.3 ± 8.8; CA3: 46.3 ± 5.3; CA2: 48.2 ± 8.6; CA1: 14.6 ± 3.5; p = 0.0006; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1E.

claim: Septal cholinergic axon density in CA1 is 14.6 ± 3.5.
source: Quantification of septal cholinergic axon densities in the DG, ML, CA3, CA2, and CA1 regions (n = 4 animals; four hippocampal slices/animal; DG: 8.73 ± 1.1; ML: 42.3 ± 8.8; CA3: 46.3 ± 5.3; CA2: 48.2 ± 8.6; CA1: 14.6 ± 3.5; p = 0.0006; one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 1E.

claim: Minimal c-Fos+ labeling was detected in MSDB cells of home-caged control (HCC) animals.
source: Minimal c-Fos+ labeling was detected in MSDB cells of HCC animals while a strong increase in c-Fos+ nuclei, including a subset of ChAT+ neurons, was observed 1 h after SI (Figure 2A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A strong increase in c-Fos+ nuclei, including a subset of ChAT+ neurons, was observed 1 h after social interaction.
source: Minimal c-Fos+ labeling was detected in MSDB cells of HCC animals while a strong increase in c-Fos+ nuclei, including a subset of ChAT+ neurons, was observed 1 h after SI (Figure 2A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: There was a significant increase in the percentage of MSDB c-Fos+ nuclei in animals exposed to empty arena compared to HCC.
source: In this condition, there was also a significant increase in the percentage of MSDB c-Fos+ nuclei compared to HCC (Figure 2D-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: The stimulation of c-Fos expression induced by exposure to empty arena was significantly less than that observed in response to social stimuli.
source: However, the stimulation of c-Fos expression induced by the exposure to EA was significantly less than that observed in response to social stimuli (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison shown in Figure 2G.

claim: In the empty arena condition, none of the c-Fos+ cells were ChAT+.
source: Furthermore and most interestingly, in the EA condition, none of the c-Fos+ cells were ChAT+ indicating a selective activation of MSDB cholinergic neurons in response to social stimuli (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei in MSDB of HCC animals is 0.72% ± 0.2%.
source: Aligned dot plot showing the mean percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in the MSDB of HCC, SI, and EA experimental groups (n = 4 animals/group; HCC: 0.72% ± 0.2%; SI: 6.83% ± 0.6%, p < 0.0001; HCC: 0.26% ± 0.1%; EA: 2.73% ± 0.8%, p = 0.02; SI vs EA, p = 0.0004, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2G.

claim: The percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei in MSDB of social interaction animals is 6.83% ± 0.6%.
source: Aligned dot plot showing the mean percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in the MSDB of HCC, SI, and EA experimental groups (n = 4 animals/group; HCC: 0.72% ± 0.2%; SI: 6.83% ± 0.6%, p < 0.0001; HCC: 0.26% ± 0.1%; EA: 2.73% ± 0.8%, p = 0.02; SI vs EA, p = 0.0004, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2G.

claim: The percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei in MSDB of empty arena animals is 2.73% ± 0.8%.
source: Aligned dot plot showing the mean percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in the MSDB of HCC, SI, and EA experimental groups (n = 4 animals/group; HCC: 0.72% ± 0.2%; SI: 6.83% ± 0.6%, p < 0.0001; HCC: 0.26% ± 0.1%; EA: 2.73% ± 0.8%, p = 0.02; SI vs EA, p = 0.0004, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2G.

claim: The percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in ChAT+ neurons of HCC animals is 0.29% ± 0.3%.
source: Aligned dot plot showing the mean percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in ChAT+ neurons of HCC, SI and EA experimental groups (n = 4 animals/group; HCC: 0.29% ± 0.3%; SI: 18.3% ± 3.9%, p = 0.03; Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2H.

claim: The percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in ChAT+ neurons of social interaction animals is 18.3% ± 3.9%.
source: Aligned dot plot showing the mean percentage of c-Fos+ nuclei detected in ChAT+ neurons of HCC, SI and EA experimental groups (n = 4 animals/group; HCC: 0.29% ± 0.3%; SI: 18.3% ± 3.9%, p = 0.03; Mann–Whitney test).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 2H.

claim: TeNT was efficiently expressed by ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB.
source: TeNT was efficiently expressed by ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: All ChAT+ neurons in MSDB were spontaneously active.
source: As shown in the figure, all ChAT+ neurons were spontaneously active.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings from MSDB ChAT+ neurons.

claim: No significant differences in the resting membrane potential (Vm) and in the spontaneous firing frequency between eYFP- and TeNT-expressing neurons were observed.
source: No significant differences in the resting membrane potential (Vm) and in the spontaneous firing frequency between eYFP- and TeNT-expressing neurons were observed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: TeNT-expressing neurons exhibited a significant reduction in their spike half-width and in their input resistance.
source: In addition, as already reported in cultured neurons (Dimpfel, 1979), TeNT-expressing neurons exhibited a significant reduction in their spike half-width and in their input resistance (Rin) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and a citation to previous research.

claim: TeNT-expressing mice were comparable to eYFP mice and showed a preference for the animal over the object during the sociability task.
source: During the sociability task, TeNT-expressing mice were comparable to eYFP mice and showed a preference for the animal over the object (Figure 3A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: TeNT mice did not show the typical preference for the novel subject compared to the familiar one in the social novelty task.
source: TeNT mice did not show the typical preference for the novel subject compared to the familiar one, as was the case in the control group (Figure 3C-D), indicating that the release of ACh is required for social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: The release of ACh is required for social novelty discrimination.
source: TeNT mice did not show the typical preference for the novel subject compared to the familiar one, as was the case in the control group (Figure 3C-D), indicating that the release of ACh is required for social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral data showing impairment in TeNT mice.

claim: TeNT mice did not show any impairment in the preference for the novel object in the NOR task as compared to eYFP group.
source: TeNT mice did not show any impairment in the preference for the novel object as compared to eYFP group (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The NOR task is not dependent on MSDB ChAT+ neurons.
source: Thus, the NOR task is not dependent on MSDB ChAT+ neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the lack of impairment in TeNT mice during NOR task.

claim: No differences in distance traveled, speed, or time spent in the outer or inner zone were observed between eYFP and TeNT mice in the open-field paradigm.
source: No differences in distance traveled, speed, or time spent in the outer or inner zone were observed between eYFP and TeNT mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B-D.

claim: No difference in distance traveled or speed was found between eYFP and TeNT groups during the execution of the social novelty task in the three-chamber apparatus.
source: Moreover, no difference in distance traveled or speed was found between the two groups when analyzed during the execution of the social novelty task in the three-chamber apparatus (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: TeNT is persistently expressed for months after stereotaxic injection.
source: TeNT is persistently expressed for months after stereotaxic injection (Kaspar et al., 2002), thus inducing a long lasting block of ACh release from MSDB cholinergic neurons that could account for the observed effect on social novelty task.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on TeNT expression.

claim: hM4 was efficiently expressed by ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB.
source: hM4 was efficiently expressed by ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CNO application hyperpolarized the membrane potential and reduced the firing frequency of hM4-expressing ChAT+ neurons.
source: CNO application hyperpolarized the membrane potential and reduced the firing frequency (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: In the absence of hM4, CNO at 10 µM does not alter the firing and membrane properties of hippocampal neurons.
source: It was shown that in the absence of hM4, this CNO concentration does not alter the firing and membrane properties of hippocampal neurons (Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on CNO effects.

claim: hM4 mice exhibited a preference for the animal over the object in the three-chamber sociability test.
source: When tested for sociability in the three-chamber paradigm, hM4 mice exhibited a preference for the animal over the object as was the case for the control group (Figure 4A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Following CNO treatment, hM4 mice did not show the typical preference for the novel mouse compared to the familiar one.
source: Following CNO treatment, hM4 mice did not show the typical preference for the novel mouse compared to the familiar one as observed in the control group (Figure 4C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB participate to, and are required for, social novelty discrimination.
source: These data corroborate the results obtained with TeNT, overall indicating that ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB participate to, and are required for, social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of TeNT and hM4 experiments.

claim: Social behavior induced activation of CA2 hippocampal neurons in eYFP control animals but not in hM4 mice.
source: As shown in Figure 4E-F, social behavior induced activation of CA2 hippocampal neurons in eYFP control animals but not in hM4 mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: The majority of c-Fos+ neurons in CA2 were PCP4−.
source: Interestingly, the majority of c-Fos+ neurons were PCP4− (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B) suggesting a restricted activation of a subpopulation of PCP4− principal neurons or local GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B.

claim: The vast majority of c-Fos+ neurons in CA2 was PV−.
source: Immunolabeling with parvalbumin (PV), the marker of a subpopulation of GABAergic interneurons, revealed that the vast majority of c-Fos+ neurons was PV− (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: No significant difference in c-Fos expression was observed between HCC and EA conditions in the CA2 region.
source: We did not observe a significant difference between HCC and EA conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A-B.

claim: No significant changes in c-Fos activation were observed in either CA3 or CA1 in mice of the three experimental groups (HCC, SI eYFP, SI hM4).
source: No significant changes in c-Fos activation were observed in either CA3 or CA1 in mice of the three experimental groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by c-Fos immunolabeling data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A-D.

claim: MSDB cholinergic neuron activation is elicited by social recognition tasks and is required for the downstream activation of the CA2 hippocampal region.
source: Altogether, these data reveal that MSDB cholinergic neuron activation is elicited by social recognition tasks and is required for the downstream activation of the CA2 hippocampal region.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the c-Fos expression data in CA2 following social behavior and MSDB cholinergic inhibition.

claim: hM4 mice showed a reduced interaction time with the object in the novel location in the OLT as compared to the eYFP group.
source: hM4 mice showed a reduced interaction time with the object in the novel location as compared to the eYFP group (Figure 4—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5B.

claim: The inhibition of MSDB cholinergic neurons affects spatial novelty.
source: These results suggest that the inhibition of MSDB cholinergic neurons also affects spatial novelty.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the OLT behavioral data.

claim: Both eYFP and hM4 animal groups showed a preference for the animal rather than the object in the sociability task when CNO was locally applied in CA2.
source: Both eYFP (n = 15) and hM4 (n = 14) animal groups showed a preference for the animal rather than the object (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: hM4 animals did not show any significant difference in interaction time spent with the novel and the familiar mice following local CNO administration in CA2.
source: In contrast to the control group (eYFP) hM4 animals did not show any significant difference in interaction time spent with the novel and the familiar mice, indicating that local release of ACh in the CA2 is necessary for social novelty discrimination (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Local release of ACh in the CA2 is necessary for social novelty discrimination.
source: In contrast to the control group (eYFP) hM4 animals did not show any significant difference in interaction time spent with the novel and the familiar mice, indicating that local release of ACh in the CA2 is necessary for social novelty discrimination (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral data following local CNO administration in CA2.

claim: Bath application of CNO (10 μM) had no effect on either frequency or amplitude of sIPSCs or sEPSCs in slices obtained from naive mice not expressing hM4.
source: In slices obtained from naive mice not expressing hM4, bath application of CNO (10 μM) had no effect on either frequency or amplitude of sIPSCs or sEPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: In slices obtained from hM4 mice, CNO decreased the frequency, but not the amplitude of sIPSCs.
source: In contrast, in slices obtained from hM4 mice, CNO decreased the frequency, but not the amplitude of sIPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2E-F.

claim: CNO decreased both the frequency and the amplitude of sEPSCs in slices obtained from hM4 mice.
source: Furthermore, CNO decreased both the frequency and the amplitude of sEPSCs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2G-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2G-H.

claim: ACh controls synaptic transmission in CA2.
source: These data clearly demonstrate that ACh controls synaptic transmission in CA2.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data showing CNO effects on synaptic currents in hM4 mice.

claim: DHβE-treated mice were impaired in the social novelty task compared to saline-treated animals.
source: However, when compared to saline-treated animals, DHβE-treated mice were impaired in the social novelty task (Figure 6C), indicating that nicotinic receptors are crucial for social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Nicotinic receptors are crucial for social novelty discrimination.
source: However, when compared to saline-treated animals, DHβE-treated mice were impaired in the social novelty task (Figure 6C), indicating that nicotinic receptors are crucial for social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the behavioral data showing impairment following DHβE treatment.

claim: Both groups of mice (saline and atropine) did not show differences in the sociability and social novelty tasks.
source: Both groups of mice did not show differences in the sociability (Figure 6E) and social novelty tasks (Figure 6F), indicating that muscarinic receptor activation is not required for social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Muscarinic receptor activation is not required for social novelty discrimination.
source: Both groups of mice did not show differences in the sociability (Figure 6E) and social novelty tasks (Figure 6F), indicating that muscarinic receptor activation is not required for social novelty discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the lack of behavioral effects following atropine treatment.

claim: Bath application of nicotine (1 μM) induced a significant decrease in the frequency of mIPSCs without affecting their amplitude.
source: Bath application of nicotine (1 μM) induced a significant decrease in the frequency of mIPSCs without affecting their amplitude (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: Nicotine had no effect on either frequency or amplitude of mEPSCs.
source: No effect was observed in either frequency or amplitude of mEPSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D), indicating that nAChR activation controls mainly GABAergic transmission in the CA2 region.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: nAChR activation controls mainly GABAergic transmission in the CA2 region.
source: No effect was observed in either frequency or amplitude of mEPSCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D), indicating that nAChR activation controls mainly GABAergic transmission in the CA2 region.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the differential effects of nicotine on mIPSCs versus mEPSCs.

claim: Nicotine significantly increased the frequency of sEPSCs without affecting their amplitude when recorded at ECl−.
source: Under this condition, nicotine significantly increased the frequency of sEPSCs without affecting their amplitude (Figure 7A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7A-B.

claim: In 6 out of 13 cells a partial recovery of the control frequency was obtained during nicotine washout.
source: In 6 out of 13 cells a partial recovery of the control frequency was obtained during nicotine washout (frequency: Nic: 1.45 ± 0.3 Hz, washout: 0.9 ± 0.1 Hz; p = 0.03; Wilcoxon test), ruling out a possible desensitizing effect of nicotine.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data showing partial recovery during washout.

claim: nAChRs activation augments the glutamatergic drive to CA2 principal cells via disinhibition.
source: These results suggest that nAChRs activation augments the glutamatergic drive to CA2 principal cells via disinhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the electrophysiological data showing increased sEPSC frequency with nicotine.

claim: In the presence of either MLA or DHβE nicotine did not change the frequency of sEPSCs.
source: In the presence of either MLA or DHβE nicotine did not change the frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 7C-F), indicating that both α7- and non-α7-nAChR subtypes are involved in nicotine-induced CA2 disinhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7C-F.

claim: Both α7- and non-α7-nAChR subtypes are involved in nicotine-induced CA2 disinhibition.
source: In the presence of either MLA or DHβE nicotine did not change the frequency of sEPSCs (Figure 7C-F), indicating that both α7- and non-α7-nAChR subtypes are involved in nicotine-induced CA2 disinhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the blockade of nicotine effects by both MLA and DHβE.

claim: In both CA3 and CA1 regions, nicotine significantly reduced the frequency of sEPSCs recorded at ECl− without blocking GABAergic transmission.
source: In contrast to what observed in CA2, in both CA3 and CA1 regions, nicotine significantly reduced the frequency of sEPSCs recorded at ECl− without blocking GABAergic transmission (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: CNO application depolarized the membrane and increased the frequency of spontaneous action potentials in hM3-expressing ChAT+ neurons.
source: CNO application depolarized the membrane and increased the frequency of spontaneous action potentials (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: CNO increased the frequency, but not the amplitude of sEPSCs in CA2 principal neurons in the presence of physostigmine and atropine.
source: In these conditions CNO increased the frequency, but not the amplitude of sEPSCs confirming the results obtained with nicotine (Figure 8A-B).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8A-B.

claim: CNO decreased the frequency and the amplitude of sEPSCs recorded from CA3 principal neurons.
source: In addition, as observed with nicotine, CNO decreased the frequency and the amplitude of sEPSCs recorded from CA3 principal neurons (Figure 8C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8C-D.

claim: CNO did not affect either the frequency or the amplitude of sEPSCs recorded from CA1 principal neurons.
source: In contrast with results obtained using nicotine, CNO did not affect either the frequency or the amplitude of sEPSCs recorded from CA1 principal neurons (Figure 8E-F).
evidence: This claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: The lack of CNO effect in CA1 could be explained by a smaller number of cholinergic terminals expressing hM4 in CA1, as compared to CA2 and CA3 regions.
source: This could be explained by a smaller number of cholinergic terminals expressing hM4 in CA1, as compared to CA2 and CA3 regions.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the differential effects of CNO across hippocampal regions.

claim: Brief light pulses delivered at low frequency to cholinergic neurons in the MSDB increased the firing rate of CA2 neurons.
source: Brief light pulses delivered at low frequency (5 ms duration, at 1 Hz for 30 s) to cholinergic neurons in the MSDB by an optical fiber, increased the firing rate of CA2 neurons (Figure 9B-D) without altering the intraburst frequency (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9B-D.

claim: Light stimulation of MSDB ChAT+ neurons did not alter the intraburst frequency of CA2 neurons.
source: Brief light pulses delivered at low frequency (5 ms duration, at 1 Hz for 30 s) to cholinergic neurons in the MSDB by an optical fiber, increased the firing rate of CA2 neurons (Figure 9B-D) without altering the intraburst frequency (Figure 9D).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: ACh release during light-induced ChR2 activation strongly affects the output of CA2 principal neurons.
source: This suggests that ACh release during light-induced ChR2 activation strongly affects the output of CA2 principal neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the in vivo optogenetic stimulation data.

claim: No effect was observed when light was delivered to not injected mice.
source: No effect was observed when light was delivered to not injected mice (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by control in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: A similar effect of light stimulation on CA2 neuron firing was observed when the animals were anesthetized with ketamine–xylazine.
source: These data were independent from the anesthetic used, as a similar effect was observed when the animals were anesthetized with ketamine–xylazine (Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1E-H.

claim: Photostimulation of ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB induced no significant change in the firing frequency of both CA3 and CA1 bursting cells.
source: Photostimulation of ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB induced no significant change in the firing frequency of both CA3 and CA1 bursting cells (Figure 9—figure supplement 2A-H).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiological data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 2A-H.

claim: ACh released from MSDB enhances CA2 principal cells firing via disinhibition, by activating nAChRs localized on GABAergic interneurons.
source: In line with slices recordings, these in vivo data suggest that ACh released from MSDB enhances CA2 principal cells firing via disinhibition, by activating nAChRs localized on GABAergic interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined in vivo and ex vivo electrophysiological data.

claim: Genetically targeted inactivation of CA2 principal cells leads to a loss of social memory.
source: Hitti and Siegelbaum, 2014 clearly demonstrated that genetically targeted inactivation of CA2 principal cells leads to a loss of social memory, namely the ability of an animal to recognize a conspecific.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on CA2 and social memory.

claim: Consolidation of social memory strictly depends on reactivation of CA2 pyramidal cell ensembles during sharp-wave ripples.
source: More recently, evidence was provided that consolidation of social memory strictly depends on reactivation of CA2 pyramidal cell ensembles during sharp-wave ripples (Oliva et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on CA2 and memory consolidation.

claim: Deficits in cholinergic transmission are associated with cognitive impairments in various forms of neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: This signaling pathway is known to be involved in several cognitive processes (for review see Ballinger et al., 2016; Solari and Hangya, 2018), and deficits in cholinergic transmission are associated with cognitive impairments in various forms of neuropsychiatric disorders (for review see Dineley et al., 2015; Terry and Callahan, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on cholinergic transmission and neuropsychiatric disorders.

claim: An increased level of ACh in the hippocampus during object exploration was not related to object familiarity or novelty.
source: This result is in agreement with findings demonstrating that an increased level of ACh in the hippocampus during object exploration was not related to object familiarity or novelty (Stanley et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on ACh and object exploration.

claim: ACh released in the perirhinal cortex plays a major role in the novel object discrimination task by acting via mAChRs.
source: Furthermore, ACh released in the perirhinal cortex seems to play a major role in the novel object discrimination task by acting via mAChRs (Winters et al., 2006; Balderas et al., 2012) rather than nAChRs (Tinsley et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on ACh in perirhinal cortex and object discrimination.

claim: ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB were selectively eliminated using a genetic cell targeting technique, resulting in deficits in OLT.
source: This result is in agreement with a previous study, whereby ChAT+ neurons in the MSDB were selectively eliminated using a genetic cell targeting technique (Okada et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on MSDB ChAT+ neuron elimination.

claim: Deficits in OLT were observed in mice lacking the M2 mAChR subtype.
source: Deficits in OLT were also observed in mice lacking the M2 mAChR subtype suggesting the involvement of these receptors in this task (Romberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on M2 mAChR and OLT.

claim: Exposure to a novel context elicits learning-dependent transcription of the immediate-early gene Arc in the CA2 region of rodents.
source: Previous studies (Wintzer et al., 2014; Alexander et al., 2016) demonstrated that exposure to a novel context elicits learning-dependent transcription of the immediate-early gene Arc in the CA2 region of rodents.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on Arc expression in CA2.

claim: The lack of β2 nAChR subtype affects social interaction during aggressive behavior.
source: In particular, the lack of β2 nAChR subtype was shown to affect social interaction during aggressive behavior (Granon et al., 2003), an effect likely involving the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC; Avale et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on β2 nAChR and social behavior.

claim: The lack of β4 nAChR subunit leads to a decreased interaction between a resident and juvenile intruder mouse.
source: The lack of β4 nAChR subunit that is highly expressed in the olfactory bulb and in the lateral habenula (Salas et al., 2003), leads to a decreased interaction between a resident and juvenile intruder mouse (Salas et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on β4 nAChR and social interaction.

claim: A single nucleotide polymorphism in the α5 subunit of nAChRs, observed in patients affected by schizophrenia, leads to deficits in sociability when engineered in mice.
source: Furthermore, a single nucleotide polymorphism in the α5 subunit of nAChRs, observed in patients affected by schizophrenia (Schizophrenia Working Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2014), leads to deficits in sociability when engineered in mice (Koukouli et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on α5 nAChR polymorphism and sociability.

claim: Activation of nAChRs by low concentration of nicotine enhances GABA release in CA3 either directly or indirectly, via NMDA receptors localized on GABAergic interneurons.
source: Similarly, in CA3 principal cells, activation of nAChRs by low concentration of nicotine enhances GABA release either directly (Hajós et al., 2005) or indirectly, via NMDA receptors localized on GABAergic interneurons (Mann and Mody, 2010; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on nicotine effects in CA3.

claim: Brain states associated with high cholinergic activity and theta oscillations resulted in CA3 principal neuron inhibition via activation of interneurons.
source: Furthermore, previous studies showed that brain states associated with high cholinergic activity and theta oscillations resulted in CA3 principal neuron inhibition via activation of interneurons (Malezieux et al., 2020; Dannenberg et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research on cholinergic activity and CA3 inhibition.

claim: A disinhibitory effect of ACh was observed in the prelimbic area of mPFC, where α5 nAChR-dependent activation of VIP+ interneurons inhibited downstream SOM+ cells, leading to an enhancement of principal neuron firing in layer 2/3.
source: Interestingly a disinhibitory effect of ACh was also observed in the prelimbic area of mPFC, where α5 nAChR-dependent activation of VIP+ interneurons inhibited downstream SOM+ cells, which in turn led to an enhancement of principal neuron firing in layer 2/3 (Koukouli et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous research on ACh disinhibition in mPFC.
